M1.S3.T3.C14.name: Isosceles Right Triangles, Q1
M1.S3.T3.C14.q: Earlier, we saw a method to create a square with double the area of a given square paper. There is another method to do this in which two identical square papers are cut in the following way: each square is cut along one diagonal, into pieces 1 and 2, and 3 and 4. Can you arrange these pieces to create a square with double the area of either square?
steps: Each square is cut along one diagonal into 2 congruent right triangles: 4 triangles in all.
Each triangle has two sides equal to the side of the square, with a right angle between them.
Put the four right angles together at one point: four right angles fill the full turn around it with no gap.
The four long sides, each a diagonal of the square, form the outside: a square whose side is the diagonal.
It is made of the 4 triangles of two squares, so its area is double either square.
M1.S3.T3.C14.ans: Yes: put the four right-angle corners together at the centre; the four diagonals make a square with double the area

M2.S7.T7.C31.name: Isosceles Right Triangles, Q3
M2.S7.T7.C31.q: The hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle is 10. What are its other two sidelengths? [Hint: Find the area of the square composed of two such right triangles.]
steps: Two such triangles make a square whose diagonal is the hypotenuse, 10.
The square on the hypotenuse has area 10 × 10 = 100.
The square made of the two triangles has half that area: 100 ÷ 2 = 50.
Its side is an equal side of the triangle, so each equal side is √50.
M2.S7.T7.C31.ans: Each of the other two sides is √50, between 7.07 and 7.08

M3.S9.T9.C40.name: Missing Sides and New Squares, Q3
M3.S9.T9.C40.q: Using the constructions you have now seen, how would you construct a square whose area is triple the area of a given square? Five times the area of a given square? (Baudhāyana's Śulba-Sūtra, Verse 1.10)
steps: Let the given square have side a and area a².
Its diagonal d is the side of the square with double the area: d² = 2a².
Make a right triangle with perpendicular sides a and d.
The square on its hypotenuse has area a² + 2a² = 3a²: triple.
For five times, make a right triangle with perpendicular sides a and 2a.
The square on its hypotenuse has area a² + 4a² = 5a².
M3.S9.T9.C40.ans: Triple: the square on the hypotenuse of the right triangle whose sides are a side and a diagonal of the given square. Five times: the square on the hypotenuse of the right triangle with sides a and 2a

M3.S9.T9.C41.name: Chapter Exercises, Q7
M3.S9.T9.C41.q: Construct a square whose area is equal to the difference of the areas of squares of sidelengths 5 units and 7 units.
steps: Draw a side of 5 units, a right angle at one end, and swing an arc of radius 7 from the other end to meet the perpendicular: a right triangle with hypotenuse 7 and one side 5.
Its third side b has b² = 7² − 5², which is 24.
The square on that third side has area 24 square units.
M3.S9.T9.C41.ans: The square on the third side of the right triangle with hypotenuse 7 and one side 5: area 24 square units

M3.S11.T11.C45.name: Using Baudhāyana's Theorem, Worked Example
M3.S11.T11.C45.q: A right-angled triangle has shorter sides 3 cm and 4 cm. Find the hypotenuse.
steps: The right angle is between the sides 3 cm and 4 cm, so the hypotenuse is the third side.

M3.S11.T11.C46.name: Missing Sides and New Squares, Q1
M3.S11.T11.C46.q: If a right-angled triangle has shorter sides of lengths 5 cm and 12 cm, then what is the length of its hypotenuse? First draw the right-angled triangle with these sidelengths and measure the hypotenuse, then check your answer using Baudhāyana's Theorem.
steps: Draw sides of 5 cm and 12 cm at a right angle and join their ends; the join measures about 13 cm.
Both shorter sides are known, so add their squares.

M3.S11.T11.C47.name: Missing Sides and New Squares, Q2
M3.S11.T11.C47.q: If a right-angled triangle has a short side of length 8 cm and hypotenuse of length 17 cm, what is the length of the third side? Again, try drawing the triangle and measuring, and then check your answer using Baudhāyana's Theorem.
steps: Draw a side of 8 cm, a right angle at one end, and swing an arc of 17 cm from the other end; the third side measures about 15 cm.
The hypotenuse is given, so subtract.

M3.S11.T11.C48.name: Missing Sides and New Squares, Q4
M3.S11.T11.C48.q: Let a, b and c denote the length of the sides of a right triangle, with c being the length of the hypotenuse. Find the missing sidelength in each of the following cases: (i) a = 5, b = 7 (ii) a = 8, b = 12 (iii) a = 9, c = 15 (iv) a = 7, b = 12 (v) a = 1.5, b = 3.5
steps: (i) Both sides at the right angle are known, so add.
(ii) Both sides at the right angle are known, so add.
(iii) The hypotenuse c is given, so subtract.
(iv) Both sides at the right angle are known, so add.
(v) Both sides at the right angle are known, so add.
M3.S11.T11.C48.ans: (i) c = √74, between 8.6 and 8.7; (ii) c = √208, between 14.4 and 14.5; (iii) b = 12; (iv) c = √193, between 13.8 and 13.9; (v) c = √14.5, between 3.8 and 3.9

M3.S11.T11.C49.name: Chapter Exercises, Q2
M3.S11.T11.C49.q: Find the missing sidelengths in the following right triangles: (a) a tilted right triangle with sides 7 and 9 at the right angle. (b) a thin tilted right triangle with sides 4 and 10 at the right angle. (c) a long thin right triangle with the right angle at its far-left corner: one side at the right angle is 40 and the side opposite the right angle is 41. (d) a right triangle with the right angle at the top: one side at the right angle is 10 and the side opposite the right angle is √200. (e) a tilted right triangle with sides 10 and √150 at the right angle. (f) a right triangle with the right angle at the bottom left: the upright side is 27 and the side opposite the right angle is 45.
steps: (a) The right angle is between the sides 7 and 9, so the missing side faces it: the hypotenuse.
(b) The right angle is between the sides 4 and 10, so the missing side is the hypotenuse.
(c) The side 41 faces the right angle, so it is the hypotenuse; subtract.
(d) The side √200 faces the right angle, so it is the hypotenuse; subtract.
(d) 10² = 100, so the missing side is 10: the triangle is isosceles.
(e) The right angle is between the sides 10 and √150, so the missing side is the hypotenuse.
(f) The side 45 faces the right angle, so it is the hypotenuse; subtract.

M3.S11.T11.C50.name: Chapter Exercises, Q4
M3.S11.T11.C50.q: Is the hypotenuse the longest side of a right triangle? Justify your answer.
steps: In a right triangle, c² = a² + b².
b² is more than 0, so c² is more than a², and so c is more than a.
In the same way c² is more than b², so c is more than b.
So the hypotenuse is longer than each of the other two sides.
M3.S11.T11.C50.ans: Yes: c² = a² + b² is bigger than a² and bigger than b², so c is the longest side

M3.S13.T13.C65.name: Triples, Q2
M3.S13.T13.C65.q: Does this method yield non-primitive Baudhāyana triples? [Hint: Observe that among the triples generated, one of the smaller sidelengths is one less than the hypotenuse.]
steps: Every triple from the method has the form (the root of the odd square, n − 1, n).
Any common factor of n − 1 and n also divides their difference, which is 1.
So n − 1 and n share no factor greater than 1, and neither can the whole triple.
M3.S13.T13.C65.ans: No: every triple the method gives is primitive

M3.S13.T13.C66.name: Triples, Q3
M3.S13.T13.C66.q: Are there primitive triples that cannot be obtained through this method? If yes, give examples.
steps: The method gives only triples in which the hypotenuse is 1 more than a side.
In none of them is the hypotenuse 1 more than a side, so the method misses them.

M3.S13.T13.C67.name: Chapter Exercises, Q5
M3.S13.T13.C67.q: True or False: Every Baudhāyana triple is either a primitive triple or a scaled version of a primitive triple.
steps: Take any triple (a, b, c) and let f be the greatest common factor of a, b and c.
If f = 1, the triple is primitive.
If f is more than 1, then (a/f, b/f, c/f) is a triple with no common factor greater than 1: a primitive triple.
And (a, b, c) is f times that primitive triple: a scaled version.

M3.S13.T13.C68.name: Chapter Exercises, Q6
M3.S13.T13.C68.q: Give 5 examples of rectangles whose sidelengths and diagonals are all integers.
steps: The diagonal of a rectangle is the hypotenuse of the right triangle made by two of its sides.
So the two sides and the diagonal must form a Baudhāyana triple.

M4.S16.T16.C73.name: A Problem from Bhāskarāchārya's Līlāvatī, Worked Example
M4.S16.T16.C73.q: A lotus tip is 1 unit above the water. Swayed by the breeze, the tip touches the water 3 units from its original position. Find the depth of the lake.
steps: Let the depth be x; the stem has length x + 1.
The upright stem is perpendicular to the water, so there is a right angle at the water surface.
The bent stem, of length x + 1, is the hypotenuse; the other sides are x and 3.

M4.S16.T16.C74.name: Chapter Exercises, Q3
M4.S16.T16.C74.q: Find the sidelength of a rhombus whose diagonals are of length 24 units and 70 units.
steps: The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles.
They cut the rhombus into 4 congruent right triangles with sides 24 ÷ 2 = 12 and 70 ÷ 2 = 35.
Each side of the rhombus is the hypotenuse of one of them.

M4.S16.T16.C75.name: Chapter Exercises, Q8
M4.S16.T16.C75.q: Using the dots of a grid as the vertices, can you create a square that has an area of (a) 2 sq. units, (b) 3 sq. units, (c) 4 sq. units, and (d) 5 sq. units? Suppose the grid extends indefinitely. What are the possible integer-valued areas of squares you can create in this manner?
steps: (i) A square with its corners on grid dots has a side that goes p dots across and q dots up, so its area is p² + q².
(i) (a) p = 1, q = 1: 1² + 1² = 2, a tilted square of area 2.
(i) (c) p = 2, q = 0: an upright 2 by 2 square, area 4.
(i) (d) p = 1, q = 2: 1² + 2² = 5, a tilted square of area 5.
(i) (b) 3 is not a sum of two squares: 0 + 1, 1 + 1, 0 + 4 and 1 + 4 give 1, 2, 4 and 5, never 3.
(ii) Every such square has area p² + q², where p and q are whole numbers of grid steps.
(ii) Numbers such as 3, 6, 7, 11, 12, 14 and 15 are not sums of two squares, so no grid square has those areas.
M4.S16.T16.C75.ans: (i) Yes for areas 2, 4 and 5; no square of area 3 is possible; (ii) Exactly the counting numbers that are a sum of two squares: 1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10, 13, 16, 17, 18, 20, 25 and so on

M4.S16.T16.C76.name: Chapter Exercises, Q9
M4.S16.T16.C76.q: Find the area of an equilateral triangle with sidelength 6 units. [Hint: Show that an altitude bisects the opposite side. Use this to find the height.]
steps: Drop the altitude from the top vertex to the base; it makes two right triangles.
They have equal hypotenuses (6), the altitude in common and right angles, so they are congruent and the altitude bisects the base into 3 and 3.
In one right triangle: 6² − 3² = 36 − 9 = 27, so h² = 27 and h = √27.
